Expected outcome: The network recognizes the correct device without address or access conflicts.

steps.title: 11. Evaluate Serial Communication Components
steps.instructions: For serial data connections, inspect the complete path, including the approved serial cable, connector seating, null-modem or straight-through configuration, serial-to-network converter, device adapter, power supply for the converter, and receiving-system input. Confirm that baud rate, parity, stop bits, and other serial settings match the approved integration documentation. Swap an external converter or adapter only with a verified equivalent that has been configured for the same connection. Expected outcome: The serial communication path and its external interface components are verified.

steps.title: 12. Perform a Controlled Restart Only When Safe
steps.instructions: Restarting the Infinity C500 or Babylog VN500 can interrupt ventilation, monitoring, alarms, and data output. Perform a restart only after the device has been removed from patient use, respiratory therapy has approved the action, required patient data has been documented, the communication infrastructure has been checked, and hospital procedures permit the restart. After startup, verify normal local operation before testing external communication. If communication returns, continue observing the connection long enough to confirm that the failure does not recur. Expected outcome: A temporary software or interface lockup is cleared without exposing a patient to risk.

steps.title: 13. Verify Communication With the Receiving System
steps.instructions: Confirm that the destination system receives the correct device identity, current parameter values, updated timestamps, continuous data, and the correct patient or bed association, when applicable. Do not consider the repair complete based only on a network link light. Verify actual data at the receiving endpoint. If communication is restored, document the cause and corrective action, complete functional verification, and return the device to service. Expected outcome: Accurate Babylog VN500 data reaches the intended destination consistently.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Babylog VN500 was operating normally but ventilation data was no longer appearing in the device-integration system.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found the Ethernet cable at the Infinity C500 was damaged and would not maintain a stable network link.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced the damaged cable with an approved known-good cable, verified current ventilator data at the receiving system, completed functional checks, and returned the device to service.

helpfulDetails: Wall jack or switch port tested

title: Drager Babylog VN500 Ventilator - CO₂ Module Not Recognized or No Capnogram
description: Troubleshooting missing CO₂ values or waveforms caused by configuration, sensor connections, airway-adapter contamination, warm-up, calibration, or defective external components.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot unreliable CO₂ monitoring while the Babylog VN500 is supporting a patient when capnography is clinically required. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team. Provide a verified independent capnography monitor. Transfer the patient to another ventilator if troubleshooting could interrupt ventilation. Confirm that ventilation, oxygenation monitoring, and local ventilator alarms remain functional. Do not disconnect the patient circuit or airway adapter without clinical authorization. Expected outcome: The patient remains safely monitored without relying on the affected CO₂ function. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only when the ventilator and CO₂ components can be evaluated safely.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Failure
steps.instructions: Determine whether: The CO₂ function or parameter is unavailable. The sensor is not recognized. A CO₂ value appears without a capnogram. The capnogram is intermittent, distorted, or flat. A warm-up, calibration, zeroing, adapter, or sensor message is displayed. The failure began after changing the patient circuit, airway adapter, or CO₂ sensor. Record the complete displayed message and alarm behavior. Expected outcome: The failure is clearly identified as a detection, configuration, signal, or accessory problem.

steps.title: 3. Verify That CO₂ Monitoring Is Enabled
steps.instructions: Review the monitoring configuration and confirm that: CO₂ monitoring is enabled. The CO₂ parameter is selected for display. A capnogram waveform is assigned to the active screen layout. Alarm limits are configured appropriately for testing. The selected patient category and ventilation configuration support the intended CO₂ setup. Do not change clinical ventilation settings solely to make the waveform appear. Expected outcome: The CO₂ parameter and waveform are enabled and visible on the selected display. If the waveform appears normally, confirm operation and stop.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the CO₂ Sensor Connection
steps.instructions: Trace the CO₂ sensor cable from the airway sensor to its designated connection. Check for: A loose or partially inserted connector. Bent, recessed, contaminated, or damaged contacts. A cable under tension. Pinched, crushed, or sharply bent cable sections. Damage near the sensor head or connector strain relief. Connection through an incorrect or unsupported interface. Disconnect and reconnect the cable only when the device is safely removed from patient use. Ensure the connector is fully seated without forcing it. Expected outcome: The sensor is securely connected and recognized by the ventilator. If recognition returns, allow the sensor to initialize and stop.

steps.title: 5. Allow the Sensor to Warm Up
steps.instructions: After connecting the CO₂ sensor, allow sufficient time for initialization and warm-up. Observe whether: A warm-up message clears. The CO₂ value becomes available. A waveform appears after several breaths during an approved test. The ventilator continues to report that the sensor is unavailable. Avoid repeatedly disconnecting the sensor during initialization. Expected outcome: The warm-up indication clears and the CO₂ sensor becomes ready for measurement.

steps.title: 6. Inspect the Airway Adapter
steps.instructions: Remove the airway adapter from clinical use and inspect it under adequate lighting. Check for: Condensation or water droplets. Mucus, secretions, or medication residue. Cracks or damaged optical windows. Incorrect adapter orientation. An adapter that is not fully seated in the sensor. Use of an incompatible, reused, or damaged adapter. Excessive dead space or an adapter inappropriate for the neonatal application. Replace a contaminated or questionable adapter with a clean, approved adapter. Do not attempt to scrape or mechanically clean optical windows. Expected outcome: A clean, intact, correctly installed airway adapter provides a clear optical measurement path. If the capnogram returns, confirm stable operation and stop.

steps.title: 7. Inspect and Reseat the CO₂ Sensor
steps.instructions: Inspect the sensor head for: Contamination around the adapter opening. Cracked housing. Loose components. Evidence of impact. Fluid intrusion. Unusual heat, odor, or discoloration. Confirm that the sensor is fully engaged with the airway adapter and positioned according to its intended orientation. Do not immerse the sensor or apply unapproved cleaning agents. Expected outcome: The sensor is clean, undamaged, and properly seated on the adapter.

steps.title: 8. Perform the Approved CO₂ Zeroing or Calibration Procedure
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use, follow the device prompts for the approved CO₂ zeroing or calibration procedure. Before beginning: Remove the sensor from the patient circuit as directed. Keep the airway adapter free from exhaled gas. Prevent anyone from breathing near or through the adapter. Allow the sensor to complete warm-up. Do not move or disturb the sensor during the procedure. If zeroing or calibration completes successfully, reconnect the sensor to an approved test setup and confirm a stable waveform. Expected outcome: The procedure completes without an error and the sensor produces a plausible CO₂ response. If zeroing or calibration repeatedly fails, continue troubleshooting.

steps.title: 9. Test With Known-Good External Components
steps.instructions: When available, substitute one component at a time: Known-good compatible airway adapter. Known-good compatible CO₂ sensor and cable. Repeat the warm-up and approved zeroing procedure after substitution. Do not replace multiple components simultaneously unless required for safety. Changing one component at a time helps identify the actual cause. Expected outcome: The failed accessory is isolated without opening the ventilator. If the known-good sensor works, remove the original sensor or cable from service.

steps.title: 10. Check for Moisture and Circuit Conditions
steps.instructions: Inspect the breathing circuit and humidification setup for conditions that could repeatedly contaminate the airway adapter. Check for: Excessive condensation. Water collecting near the CO₂ adapter. A saturated filter. Incorrect circuit orientation. A water trap that is full or incorrectly positioned. Aerosol or secretion accumulation across the optical path. Clinical staff must approve any change to the patient circuit configuration. Expected outcome: Moisture or contamination is not obstructing the CO₂ measurement path.

steps.title: 11. Perform an Operational Verification
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to an approved test lung and compatible test setup. Confirm that: The CO₂ sensor remains recognized. A waveform appears consistently. The numerical value responds appropriately to a controlled CO₂ source, when available. The displayed waveform does not drop out when the cable is gently repositioned. No CO₂-related alarms or technical messages return. Ventilator operation and local alarms remain normal. Do not return the device to clinical service based only on the disappearance of an error message. Expected outcome: CO₂ detection, waveform display, and associated alarms operate consistently during testing. If the device passes, document the findings and return it according to facility policy.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Drager Babylog VN500 did not recognize the CO₂ sensor and displayed no capnogram.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found condensation inside the neonatal airway adapter, obstructing the CO₂ sensor’s optical measurement path.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the contaminated adapter, installed a compatible clean adapter, completed CO₂ zeroing, and verified a stable capnogram using an approved test setup.

helpfulDetails: Exact CO₂ message or alarm displayed
Whether the numerical value, waveform, or both were missing
Intermittent response when the cable was moved
Unusual heat, odor, or physical damage

title: Drager Babylog VN500 Ventilator - Startup Failure, Boot Loop, or Software Freeze
description: Troubleshooting failed startup, repeated restarting, frozen controls, or an unresponsive display caused by power, connections, accessories, environment, or internal system faults.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a startup failure, boot loop, or frozen Babylog VN500 while a patient depends on it for ventilation. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team immediately. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Provide manual ventilation when clinically required and performed by qualified personnel. Confirm adequate ventilation, oxygenation, and independent monitoring before continuing. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on an unavailable or unreliable ventilator. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the Babylog VN500 has been removed from patient use. The manufacturer directs users to disconnect the patient and use another independent ventilator for startup, system, safety-software, or internal-communication failures.

steps.title: 2. Identify the Exact Startup Behavior
steps.instructions: Observe and document what happens when the device is powered on: No lights, sounds, or screen activity; Power indicators illuminate, but the display remains blank; Startup logo appears and remains displayed; Device repeatedly restarts; Infinity C500 display starts, but the ventilation unit does not; Ventilation unit starts, but the display remains unavailable; Screen loads but freezes before reaching the standby screen; Touchscreen or rotary knob becomes unresponsive; A numbered “Device failure” or technical message appears; Freeze occurs only after connecting a particular accessory. Photograph or record the complete error message and failure number when permitted by hospital policy. Expected outcome: The failure is categorized as a power, display, communication, accessory, or internal system problem.

steps.title: 3. Check the AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Verify that the ventilator is connected directly to a known-good hospital-grade outlet. Confirm that the power cord is fully seated at the ventilator and wall outlet. Inspect the plug and cord for cuts, bent blades, discoloration, looseness, or heat damage. Test the outlet with an approved electrical safety analyzer or outlet tester. Avoid troubleshooting through an extension cord, switched outlet, or questionable power strip. Check whether the mains-power indicator illuminates. The Babylog VN500 normally uses mains power first and then available battery sources. The mains indicator should illuminate when AC power is present and the device toggle switch is on. Expected outcome: Stable AC power is confirmed. If correcting the outlet or power-cord connection allows the unit to complete startup normally, perform the required operational checks and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Main Power Switch Position
steps.instructions: Open the left-side device flap and verify that the main toggle switch is in the on position. Do not repeatedly or forcefully operate the switch. Check that: The switch remains firmly in position; The surrounding area is undamaged; No liquid, debris, or physical damage is visible; The side flap has not pressed against or disturbed the switch. The manufacturer’s startup sequence requires the mains plug to be connected, the ventilation-unit toggle switch to be on, and the power key on the Infinity C500 to be pressed. Expected outcome: The ventilation unit is properly enabled for startup.

steps.title: 5. Check Battery and Power Indicators
steps.instructions: Observe the internal battery and optional PS500 power-supply indicators, when equipped. Look for: No battery indicator; Fault indication; Severely discharged battery; Rapidly changing power status; Restarting when transitioning between AC and battery; Evidence that the device was stored disconnected from AC for an extended period. Connect the device to verified AC power and allow a severely depleted battery to charge according to facility procedures before retesting. Do not assume a battery fault is the sole cause of a boot loop when stable AC power is available. Expected outcome: The device receives stable power without cycling between power sources.

steps.title: 6. Allow the Device to Reach Room Conditions
steps.instructions: Determine whether the ventilator was recently moved from: A cold storage room; A delivery vehicle; An outdoor environment; A hot or humid location; An area with significant temperature differences. Inspect for visible condensation. Do not power the device when condensation may be present. The manufacturer warns that switching on the device after movement from cold storage into a warm environment may adversely affect proper operation; condensation must be allowed to dry first. Expected outcome: Environmental conditions are within the facility’s acceptable operating range and no condensation is present.

steps.title: 7. Inspect External System Connections
steps.instructions: With the device powered down and disconnected from patient use, inspect the externally accessible connections between: Infinity C500 operating and display unit; Babylog VN500 ventilation unit; PS500 power-supply unit, when installed; GS500 gas-supply unit, when installed; System power and communication cables; Equipotential grounding connection; Network and serial-data cables; Nurse-call cable; USB devices. Look for: Loose or partially seated connectors; Bent pins; Damaged locking mechanisms; Pinched or stretched cables; Liquid contamination; Cables pulled tight by cart movement; Connectors disturbed during cleaning or transport. Reseat only user-accessible connectors approved for routine Clinical Engineering handling. Do not open covers or disconnect internal harnesses. Expected outcome: All required external power and communication connections are secure and undamaged. If reseating an approved external connection restores normal startup, complete the device and breathing-circuit checks before returning the unit to service.

steps.title: 8. Disconnect Nonessential External Accessories
steps.instructions: With the ventilator off, temporarily disconnect nonessential external devices one at a time, such as: USB storage devices; Network cable; Serial-data adapter; Nurse-call cable; External monitoring interface; CO₂ monitoring accessory; Nebulizer accessory; Other recently installed optional equipment. Do not disconnect required system cables between the display, ventilation unit, or power-supply components. Attempt one controlled startup after unnecessary accessories have been removed. Expected outcome: The ventilator completes startup without being affected by a defective or incompatible external accessory. If startup succeeds, reconnect accessories individually to identify the component associated with the freeze. Replace or evaluate that accessory before further use.

steps.title: 9. Inspect the Display and Controls
steps.instructions: Check the Infinity C500 for: Cracked display glass; Evidence of liquid intrusion; A control continuously touching the screen; Objects resting against the touchscreen; A rotary knob that is stuck or continuously pressed; Damaged power or alarm-silence keys; Loose mounting hardware placing stress on the display assembly. Remove protective films, labels, residue, or objects that may cause unintended touchscreen input. Do not press multiple controls repeatedly during startup. A stuck or continuously pressed rotary knob can generate a fault condition. Expected outcome: No external obstruction or mechanically stuck control is interfering with startup.

steps.title: 10. Perform One Controlled Power Cycle
steps.instructions: Only after the ventilator is off the patient and external checks are complete: Attempt the normal shutdown process if the interface responds; If the device is frozen and cannot be shut down normally, place the left-side toggle switch in the off position; Disconnect the AC mains plug; Wait long enough for screen and indicator activity to stop completely; Reconnect the mains plug; Place the toggle switch in the on position; Press the power key on the Infinity C500; Observe the complete startup sequence without repeatedly pressing controls. The manufacturer provides the toggle-switch procedure when a device malfunction prevents normal shutdown. Turning off the toggle switch alone does not completely isolate the device from mains voltage; complete disconnection requires unplugging the mains plug. Expected outcome: The ventilator completes a single stable startup and reaches the expected standby or patient-selection screen. Do not repeatedly cycle power when the same boot loop or technical failure returns.

steps.title: 11. Record Any Device-Failure Number
steps.instructions: If the ventilator displays a numbered failure, document it exactly. Relevant startup-related messages may include: Device failure (3): Internal communication failure; Device failure (4): System data storage-media failure; Device failure (9): No mass-storage device found; Device failure (10): Safety-software failure; Device failure (11): Failure detected during startup; Device failure (12): System failure; Restart of ventilation unit delayed: Technical failure detected. These conditions require manufacturer-authorized service rather than repeated user-level recovery attempts. Expected outcome: The exact failure code is available for repair triage and manufacturer support.

steps.title: 12. Run the Required System Checks After Recovery
steps.instructions: If the ventilator starts normally and remains responsive: Confirm that the display, touchscreen, rotary knob, alarm indicators, and audible alarms function; Verify that the ventilation unit is recognized; Review the event and alarm history when accessible; Perform the device check; Perform the breathing-circuit check using the correct test lung and circuit configuration; Verify operation on AC and the approved battery-transfer check; Confirm that no startup, communication, temperature, storage, or system alarms return; Allow the unit to remain operating on a test circuit long enough to identify an intermittent freeze or restart. The manufacturer requires a device check before patient use and instructs that a malfunction found during the check must be corrected before use. Expected outcome: The Babylog VN500 starts consistently, passes required checks, and operates without freezing or restarting. If the problem returns at any point, stop testing and escalate the device for repair.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Drager Babylog VN500 repeatedly displayed the startup screen, restarted, and would not reach the standby screen.
CCR.Cause: Verified AC power and external connections; the boot loop remained and the ventilator displayed Device failure (11), indicating a failure detected during startup.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the ventilator from service, applied an Out of Service label, documented the failure code, and forwarded the unit for manufacturer-authorized bench repair.

helpfulDetails: Number and wording of displayed failure
Whether the display or ventilation unit restarted
Evidence of condensation or recent transport
Recent cleaning, software work, or accessory installation
Whether the fault returned during extended testing

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Air or O2 Gas Supply Failure
description: Addresses loss or interruption of ventilator air or oxygen supply caused by source, hose, connection, infrastructure, or equipment-related problems.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Ventilation
steps.instructions: Treat any loss of required ventilator gas supply as a patient-safety issue. If ventilation or oxygen delivery is unreliable, immediately transition the patient to a verified alternative ventilator or backup ventilation method. Do not disconnect a gas source from a ventilator supporting a patient solely for troubleshooting. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation and oxygenation continue without dependence on the affected gas supply path.

steps.title: 2. Confirm Which Gas Supply Is Affected
steps.instructions: Identify whether the ventilator reports an air supply problem, oxygen supply problem, or both. Record any displayed message exactly. Determine whether the failure is continuous or intermittent. Expected outcome: The affected supply path is identified.

steps.title: 3. Inspect Gas Hose Connections
steps.instructions: Trace the affected hose from the ventilator to the source. Verify secure connections at both ends and inspect for kinks, crushing, visible damage, contamination, or loose fittings. Expected outcome: The hose is securely connected and unobstructed. If restoring a loose connection clears the condition, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 4. Verify the Gas Source
steps.instructions: Check the wall outlet, cylinder-based source, or other approved supply using the facility's accepted method. If another verified source is available, compare ventilator operation using that source. Expected outcome: The external source is confirmed available. If the original outlet or source is faulty, remove it from use and report the infrastructure problem.

steps.title: 5. Check for Incorrect or Interchanged Connections
steps.instructions: Confirm that the air and oxygen hoses are connected to their intended sources and ventilator inlets. Do not assume labeling alone proves correct connection; visually trace the complete supply path. Expected outcome: Air and oxygen supply paths are correctly connected.

steps.title: 6. Inspect Hose and Connector Condition
steps.instructions: Examine accessible hose fittings, adapters, and ventilator gas inlets for physical damage or abnormal wear. Substitute a known-good approved hose if the existing hose is questionable. Expected outcome: The gas supply fault resolves with the known-good hose, identifying the original external component as the cause.

steps.title: 7. Compare With Another Device or Outlet
steps.instructions: When infrastructure is suspected, compare the affected outlet with another known-good outlet or another suitable device according to facility policy. Coordinate infrastructure findings with Facilities or the appropriate medical-gas service group. Expected outcome: The fault is isolated to either the external gas infrastructure or the ventilator.

steps.title: 8. Restart and Recheck Off Patient
steps.instructions: After gas supplies are verified and the patient is no longer dependent on the ventilator, restart or reinitialize the device if appropriate and observe whether the supply condition clears. Expected outcome: The ventilator recognizes both required gas sources and no supply fault remains.

steps.title: 9. Perform Ventilation and Oxygen Verification
steps.instructions: Use a test lung and approved test equipment to verify stable ventilator operation, gas delivery, and oxygen concentration following correction. Expected outcome: Ventilation remains stable and gas-supply indications are normal. Troubleshooting can stop when all required checks pass.

steps.title: 10. Escalate an Internal Gas-Supply Failure
steps.instructions: If verified gas sources and known-good hoses are available but the ventilator continues to report gas supply failure, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator remains out of service for qualified evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 indicated loss of oxygen supply during setup.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the external oxygen hose fitting was not fully engaged at the wall outlet.
CCR.Resolution: The connection was secured, gas supply recognition returned to normal, and ventilation and oxygen delivery were verified with test equipment before return to service.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Apnea, Low Minute Volume, or Low Tidal Volume Alarm
description: Addresses low-volume or apnea alarms caused by disconnections, leaks, circuit problems, sensing issues, settings, patient conditions, or ventilator faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Confirm Effective Ventilation
steps.instructions: Treat apnea and low-volume alarms as potentially clinical emergencies. Clinical staff should immediately assess the patient, airway, chest movement, and actual ventilation. If effective ventilation is uncertain, use an appropriate backup method or another verified ventilator. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation is maintained independently of the troubleshooting process.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Alarm
steps.instructions: Identify whether the reported condition is apnea, low minute volume, low tidal volume, or a combination. Record the exact displayed alarm and when it occurs. Expected outcome: The specific reported condition and its timing are documented.

steps.title: 3. Check for Circuit Disconnection
steps.instructions: Trace the entire breathing circuit from ventilator to patient connection. Look for loose fittings, disconnected tubing, partially separated components, or an open sampling or accessory port. Expected outcome: The breathing circuit is fully connected. If reconnecting a loose component restores ventilation and alarms clear, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 4. Check for Circuit or Airway Leaks
steps.instructions: Inspect the circuit, humidification components, tubing, adapters, and accessible connections for cracks, loose fittings, or other leakage. Patient airway and interface leakage should be evaluated by clinical staff. Expected outcome: Significant external leaks are identified and corrected.

steps.title: 5. Inspect Flow-Sensing Components
steps.instructions: Verify correct seating and condition of accessible flow measurement components. Look for contamination, moisture, or improper installation. Expected outcome: Flow sensing components are correctly installed and suitable for operation.

steps.title: 6. Verify Ventilation Settings
steps.instructions: Confirm that ventilation mode, volume or pressure settings, alarm limits, and apnea-related settings correspond to the intended clinical plan. Clinical settings should be confirmed with the responsible respiratory or medical team rather than changed solely to silence an alarm. Expected outcome: The ventilator configuration is appropriate for the intended use.

steps.title: 7. Test the Ventilator With a Test Lung
steps.instructions: Remove the ventilator from patient service before technical testing. Connect a suitable test lung and determine whether the reported low-volume or apnea condition can be reproduced. Expected outcome: Stable volume delivery and monitoring occur with the test lung. If the alarm occurs only on the patient, clinical factors should be evaluated.

steps.title: 8. Substitute Known-Good External Components
steps.instructions: If the problem persists off patient, replace questionable external components such as the breathing circuit, flow sensor, or relevant accessory with known-good approved components. Expected outcome: The fault clears when the defective external component is removed from the system.

steps.title: 9. Verify Delivered and Measured Ventilation
steps.instructions: Use appropriate approved test equipment to evaluate delivered and measured ventilation following correction. Expected outcome: Ventilation measurements are stable and alarm behavior is appropriate. Troubleshooting can stop when required verification passes.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Low-Volume or Apnea Alarms
steps.instructions: If alarms continue during controlled testing with a verified circuit and appropriate external components, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The device remains out of service for qualified technical evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported repeated low tidal volume alarms from the Evita V600.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found a loose connection in the external breathing circuit that created a significant leak.
CCR.Resolution: The circuit connection was secured, ventilation was verified with a test lung, and appropriate volume measurement and alarm operation were confirmed before return to service.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Battery Not Charging or Short Runtime
description: Addresses charging failures or reduced battery runtime caused by AC power, connections, battery condition, charging environment, configuration, or internal power faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Reliable Power
steps.instructions: Do not perform battery troubleshooting while a patient depends on an uncertain power source. Ensure the ventilator remains on reliable AC power or exchange it for another verified ventilator before testing. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation is not dependent on the questionable battery system.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Reported Battery Problem
steps.instructions: Determine whether the battery does not charge, charges intermittently, displays an abnormal status, or provides shorter runtime than expected. Record the battery indication before connecting AC power and observe whether the condition changes afterward. Expected outcome: The exact battery-related symptom is established.

steps.title: 3. Verify the AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a known-good AC receptacle. Inspect the power cord and accessible connections for looseness or physical damage. Avoid using an unverified power strip or extension source during testing. Expected outcome: Reliable AC power is supplied to the ventilator. If charging resumes normally, troubleshoot the original power source rather than the ventilator.

steps.title: 4. Confirm the Ventilator Recognizes AC Power
steps.instructions: Observe the device's normal power or charging indications after connecting verified AC power. If the device continues operating as though on battery, recheck the outlet and power cord before suspecting an internal charging failure. Expected outcome: The ventilator recognizes external power and indicates the expected charging state.

steps.title: 5. Inspect Accessible Battery Components
steps.instructions: Inspect externally accessible battery areas for incomplete seating, contamination, swelling, leakage, cracking, heat damage, or other physical abnormalities. Do not continue using a battery that appears physically damaged. Expected outcome: Battery components are correctly installed and show no unsafe physical condition.

steps.title: 6. Reseat Removable Battery Components When Applicable
steps.instructions: If the installed battery configuration allows normal external removal, reseat the battery according to approved handling practices. Expected outcome: The battery is recognized and charging resumes normally. If so, continue with verification.

steps.title: 7. Compare With a Known-Good Battery
steps.instructions: When compatible and permitted, substitute a known-good approved battery. Expected outcome: Normal charging and runtime behavior with the known-good battery indicates the original battery requires replacement.

steps.title: 8. Evaluate Charging and Runtime Under Controlled Conditions
steps.instructions: Allow the battery to charge under normal conditions, then perform an appropriate off-patient operational assessment in accordance with facility procedures. Do not invent an acceptance time if the applicable manufacturer or facility criterion is unavailable. Expected outcome: Battery performance meets the applicable documented acceptance criterion.

steps.title: 9. Verify Power Transfer and Basic Function
steps.instructions: Off patient, verify that the ventilator operates appropriately during normal transition between external power and battery power according to approved testing practices. Expected outcome: The ventilator maintains stable operation and provides expected power-status indications. Troubleshooting can stop if all applicable criteria pass.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Unresolved Charging or Runtime Failure
steps.instructions: If a known-good AC source and battery do not restore proper charging or operation, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator remains out of service until its internal power or charging system is evaluated.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 battery showed a charge but depleted unusually quickly during off-AC operation.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering confirmed reduced runtime with the installed battery and normal operation with a known-good approved battery.
CCR.Resolution: The degraded battery was replaced, charging and battery operation were verified, and the ventilator passed functional testing before return to service.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Expiratory Valve Not Recognized or Not Seated
description: Addresses expiratory valve recognition or seating problems caused by installation, contamination, moisture, damaged components, or unresolved ventilator interface faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Remove the Device From Use
steps.instructions: An expiratory valve problem can affect ventilation and pressure control. Do not troubleshoot the valve while a patient depends on the affected ventilator. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator when necessary. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation is maintained and the Evita V600 is available for safe technical evaluation.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Reported Condition
steps.instructions: Record the exact displayed message and determine whether the valve is never recognized, intermittently recognized, or reported as improperly installed. Note whether the problem began after cleaning, replacement, or reassembly. Expected outcome: The exact recognition problem is documented and reproducible.

steps.title: 3. Remove and Inspect the Expiratory Valve Assembly
steps.instructions: Using normal approved handling procedures, remove the externally removable expiratory valve assembly and inspect it for contamination, moisture, residue, cracks, deformation, or incomplete assembly. Do not perform deep disassembly or internal repair. Expected outcome: The valve assembly is visibly intact and properly prepared for installation.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Valve Receptacle and Mating Area
steps.instructions: Inspect accessible mating surfaces for moisture, debris, foreign material, or physical damage that could prevent complete seating. Do not insert tools into internal mechanisms or electrical interfaces. Expected outcome: The mounting area is clean, dry as appropriate, and unobstructed.

steps.title: 5. Reinstall the Valve Correctly
steps.instructions: Reinstall the expiratory valve according to its normal user-removable configuration and confirm that it is fully seated. Expected outcome: The ventilator recognizes the valve. If recognition returns consistently, continue to final verification.

steps.title: 6. Check Related Breathing-System Components
steps.instructions: Verify that nearby flow-sensing components, breathing circuit connections, and accessories are correctly installed and are not mechanically preventing proper valve seating. Expected outcome: The complete expiratory assembly is correctly configured.

steps.title: 7. Substitute a Known-Good Expiratory Valve
steps.instructions: Install a known-good compatible valve assembly when available. Expected outcome: If the ventilator recognizes the known-good valve consistently, the original valve assembly is the likely cause. Replace it and continue verification.

steps.title: 8. Check for Intermittent Recognition
steps.instructions: With the device off patient, perform repeated normal installation and startup checks without forcing or manipulating the connector. Expected outcome: Valve recognition remains stable through normal handling. Intermittent recognition indicates the device should not be returned to service.

steps.title: 9. Complete System and Functional Testing
steps.instructions: Run the required system or pre-use check and operate the ventilator with a test lung. Confirm stable ventilation, exhalation, pressure behavior, and alarm function. Expected outcome: The expiratory valve is recognized consistently and ventilation testing passes. Troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Recognition Failure
steps.instructions: If a known-good valve remains unrecognized or seating appears correct but the condition persists, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator remains out of service pending qualified repair evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 would not recognize the installed expiratory valve.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the removable expiratory valve was incompletely seated after reassembly.
CCR.Resolution: The valve was correctly reinstalled, recognition remained stable, and the ventilator passed the required system check and test-lung verification.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Flow Sensor Calibration Failure
description: Addresses flow sensor calibration failures caused by contamination, moisture, installation problems, damaged sensors, breathing-system setup, or unresolved service-level faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Ventilation
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot unreliable flow measurement while a patient depends on the affected ventilator. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or appropriate backup ventilation if the failure affects safe monitoring or ventilation. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation remains supported independently of the device being evaluated.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Calibration Failure
steps.instructions: Identify whether calibration will not begin, stops before completion, or completes unsuccessfully. Record any displayed message exactly. Confirm whether the problem occurs every time or began after circuit cleaning, sensor replacement, or breathing-system reassembly. Expected outcome: The failure is reproduced and its circumstances are documented.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: Remove the flow sensor only according to normal approved handling procedures. Inspect it for visible contamination, moisture, residue, damage, incorrect assembly, or deformation. Do not attempt component-level repair of the sensor. Expected outcome: The sensor is clean, dry when required, physically intact, and suitable for testing. If correcting an obvious external issue restores calibration, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 4. Verify Sensor Installation
steps.instructions: Reinstall the sensor carefully and confirm that it is fully seated and oriented correctly in its intended location. Inspect accessible mating surfaces and connections for contamination, damage, or incomplete engagement. Expected outcome: The sensor is correctly installed and securely seated. If calibration succeeds after reseating, troubleshooting can stop after final verification.

steps.title: 5. Inspect the Breathing System
steps.instructions: Check the circuit, expiratory valve, filters, humidification components, and related accessories for incorrect assembly, leaks, moisture, or obstruction that could interfere with calibration. Expected outcome: The breathing system is correctly assembled and free of obvious conditions that could affect flow measurement.

steps.title: 6. Check for Moisture or Condensation
steps.instructions: Inspect the externally accessible flow path for accumulated moisture or condensation, especially following cleaning or humidified operation. Correct moisture problems using approved handling procedures and ensure reusable components are prepared according to facility and manufacturer requirements. Expected outcome: Excess moisture is removed and components are in an appropriate condition for calibration.

steps.title: 7. Substitute a Known-Good Approved Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: If available, install a known-good compatible sensor and repeat the calibration. Do not condemn the ventilator based solely on one questionable sensor. Expected outcome: Calibration succeeds with the known-good sensor, identifying the original sensor as the likely external cause. Replace the affected sensor and proceed to verification.

steps.title: 8. Compare Against a Known-Good Setup
steps.instructions: If calibration still fails, compare the breathing-system installation and removable components with another correctly configured Evita V600. Correct only verified setup differences. Expected outcome: External configuration differences are eliminated as a cause.

steps.title: 9. Perform Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After successful calibration, operate the ventilator using appropriate test equipment or a test lung. Verify that displayed flow-related measurements respond plausibly and that ventilation is stable. Expected outcome: Calibration completes successfully and flow measurement behaves normally. Troubleshooting can stop and the ventilator may be returned to service according to policy.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Calibration Failure
steps.instructions: If calibration fails with a known-good sensor and correct external setup, discontinue external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The device remains out of clinical service until evaluated by qualified service personnel.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 repeatedly failed flow sensor calibration.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found moisture contamination on the removable flow sensor following breathing-circuit use.
CCR.Resolution: The affected sensor was replaced with an approved known-good sensor, calibration completed successfully, and ventilation was verified with a test lung.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - High Airway Pressure Alarm
description: Addresses persistent high airway pressure alarms caused by circuit obstruction, tubing problems, accessories, settings, patient-related resistance, or ventilator malfunction.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Assess the Clinical Situation
steps.instructions: A high airway pressure alarm can indicate an immediate patient or airway problem. Clinical staff should assess the patient, airway, and ventilation first. Do not troubleshoot the ventilator while a patient depends on unreliable ventilation. Exchange the device if an equipment fault is suspected and cannot be immediately ruled out. Expected outcome: The patient's ventilation and airway are safely managed before equipment troubleshooting begins.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Alarm Condition
steps.instructions: Record the exact alarm and determine whether it occurs continuously, during inspiration, only at particular settings, or only with a specific circuit or patient setup. Expected outcome: The circumstances that trigger the alarm are clearly identified.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Breathing Circuit
steps.instructions: Look for kinked tubing, compressed tubing, blocked filters, closed clamps, pooled condensate, obstructed connectors, or incorrectly installed accessories. Trace the entire inspiratory and expiratory pathway. Expected outcome: The breathing circuit is open and correctly assembled. If removing an external obstruction eliminates the alarm, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Expiratory Path
steps.instructions: Verify that the expiratory valve and associated external components are properly installed and unobstructed. Check for moisture, secretions, contamination, or incorrect seating that could increase expiratory resistance. Expected outcome: Exhaled gas has an unrestricted pathway through correctly installed external components.

steps.title: 5. Check Filters, Humidification, and Accessories
steps.instructions: Inspect filters, humidifiers, adapters, nebulizer components, and other added accessories for obstruction, saturation, incorrect orientation, or excessive resistance. Substitute known-good components when appropriate. Expected outcome: No external accessory is producing abnormal resistance. If replacing an obstructed accessory resolves the alarm, troubleshooting can stop after verification.

steps.title: 6. Verify Ventilator Settings
steps.instructions: Confirm that pressure-related limits and ventilation settings match the intended clinical configuration. Clinical settings should be evaluated in coordination with qualified clinical staff. Do not arbitrarily increase an alarm threshold to suppress a valid alarm. Expected outcome: Settings are appropriate and the alarm is not being caused by an unintended configuration.

steps.title: 7. Test the Ventilator Off Patient
steps.instructions: After removing the ventilator from patient use, connect an appropriate test lung and reproduce the operating conditions as closely as practical. Observe whether the high-pressure alarm persists without the patient. Expected outcome: If the alarm does not occur with a test lung, patient, airway, or patient-specific circuit conditions require clinical evaluation. If it persists, continue equipment troubleshooting.

steps.title: 8. Substitute the Breathing Circuit
steps.instructions: Install a known-good approved circuit and appropriate external accessories. Expected outcome: If the alarm resolves with the replacement circuit, the original circuit or accessory set was the likely cause.

steps.title: 9. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: Operate the ventilator over appropriate test conditions using a test lung and approved test equipment. Confirm appropriate pressure behavior and alarm response. Expected outcome: Ventilation is stable, pressures behave as expected, and alarm operation is functional. Troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Equipment-Related High Pressure
steps.instructions: If the high-pressure condition persists using a verified test lung, known-good circuit, correct external components, and appropriate settings, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator is removed from service for further evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported repeated high airway pressure alarms from the Evita V600.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found a saturated external breathing-circuit filter creating excessive resistance.
CCR.Resolution: The affected filter was replaced, ventilation was tested with a test lung, and normal pressure and alarm behavior were verified before return to service.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Network, Data Export, or Integrated Device Communication Failure
description: Addresses missing network communication or data transfer caused by cables, ports, connectivity, configuration, destination systems, interfaces, or infrastructure faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Preserve Clinical Monitoring
steps.instructions: Determine whether the communication failure affects only secondary data transfer or also removes clinically relied-upon remote monitoring, alarms, documentation, or integration. If remote information is unavailable, clinical staff must maintain an alternate verified monitoring and alarm-response method. Expected outcome: Patient care does not depend on the failed data connection while troubleshooting is performed.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Scope of the Failure
steps.instructions: Determine whether the issue affects network connectivity, central monitoring, EMR or device integration, data export, or a specific connected destination. Identify whether one ventilator or multiple devices are affected. Expected outcome: The affected communication path is clearly defined.

steps.title: 3. Check Local Ventilator Operation
steps.instructions: Verify that the Evita V600 itself operates normally and that the communication problem is not associated with a broader startup, display, or system fault. Expected outcome: Ventilation and local device functions remain normal.

steps.title: 4. Inspect External Communication Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect accessible network cables, interface cables, adapters, and connectors for loose connections, damage, bent hardware, or accidental disconnection. Reseat external connections when safe and appropriate. Expected outcome: All communication connections are secure and physically intact. If communication returns, verify the complete downstream path before stopping.

steps.title: 5. Test With a Known-Good Cable or Port
steps.instructions: Substitute a known-good compatible cable or connect to another approved known-good network or interface port when facility policy permits. Expected outcome: Communication returns with the known-good cable or port, isolating the fault to the external infrastructure component.

steps.title: 6. Check the Destination System
steps.instructions: Verify that the receiving system, integration gateway, monitoring station, export destination, or other connected device is online and available. Determine whether other devices using the same destination are communicating normally. Expected outcome: The downstream destination is either confirmed functional or identified as the source of the outage.

steps.title: 7. Verify Approved Communication Configuration
steps.instructions: Review accessible network or communication settings against the approved configuration or a known-good comparable Evita V600. Do not change IP addressing, integration parameters, security settings, or protected configuration values without authorization. Expected outcome: No accidental or unauthorized configuration difference is present.

steps.title: 8. Coordinate With Network or Integration Support
steps.instructions: If the physical path is intact but communication remains unavailable, coordinate with the appropriate IT, clinical integration, or infrastructure team to confirm network port status, VLAN or routing availability, interface-engine status, and receiving-system operation as applicable. Expected outcome: Infrastructure-level issues are either corrected or ruled out.

steps.title: 9. Verify the Complete Communication Path
steps.instructions: After correction, confirm that the intended data reaches the actual destination. Do not stop at a link indicator or local connectivity symbol. Where applicable, verify current data, device identity, timestamps, alarms, or exported records at the receiving endpoint. Expected outcome: End-to-end communication is restored and confirmed. Troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Device-Specific Communication Failure
steps.instructions: If a known-good cable, port, network path, destination, and approved configuration are verified but the Evita V600 still does not communicate, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator communication fault is referred for qualified service evaluation without unnecessary configuration changes.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 was operating normally but ventilator data was no longer appearing at the integrated receiving system.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found a damaged external network cable between the ventilator connection point and the approved network port.
CCR.Resolution: The cable was replaced with a known-good approved cable, end-to-end data transmission was confirmed at the receiving system, and the device was returned to service.

helpfulDetails: Whether one or multiple devices were affected

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - O2 Sensor Calibration Failure or Incorrect FiO2
description: Addresses unsuccessful oxygen calibration or questionable FiO2 readings caused by gas supply, connections, configuration, leaks, or sensing-related faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Verify Oxygenation Independently
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot questionable oxygen delivery while a patient depends on the affected ventilator. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator when delivered oxygen concentration cannot be trusted. Use appropriate independent clinical monitoring during any equipment exchange. Expected outcome: The patient is supported by equipment with verified oxygen delivery.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Reported Condition
steps.instructions: Determine whether the problem is a failed oxygen calibration, an unexpectedly high or low displayed FiO2, unstable readings, or disagreement with another measurement. Record any displayed message and the conditions under which the problem occurs. Expected outcome: The exact oxygen-related failure is identified and reproducible.

steps.title: 3. Verify Oxygen and Air Sources
steps.instructions: Confirm that both required gas supplies are connected to the intended inlets and that hoses are securely attached. Inspect the hoses and fittings for damage, kinks, loose connections, or accidental interchange. Expected outcome: Air and oxygen supplies are correctly connected and externally intact. If correcting a supply connection restores normal operation, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 4. Check the Facility Gas Source
steps.instructions: Verify the affected wall outlet or source using an appropriate facility-approved method. If practical, compare the ventilator on another known-good gas source. Do not assume the ventilator is defective when the infrastructure has not been ruled out. Expected outcome: The external oxygen and air sources supplying the ventilator are verified.

steps.title: 5. Inspect the Breathing Circuit for Leaks or Incorrect Setup
steps.instructions: Check all accessible circuit connections, humidification components, filters, valves, and accessories for leaks, disconnections, or improper assembly. Expected outcome: The breathing system is intact and correctly configured. If correcting a leak restores expected oxygen measurement, troubleshooting can stop after verification.

steps.title: 6. Verify Ventilator Settings and Configuration
steps.instructions: Confirm that the commanded oxygen setting and relevant ventilation configuration match what is expected for the test being performed. Avoid unauthorized configuration changes. Compare with an established known-good setup if needed. Expected outcome: The expected delivered oxygen concentration and configured value are understood and consistent.

steps.title: 7. Repeat Approved Oxygen Calibration
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from clinical service and external conditions verified, repeat the normal approved oxygen calibration process. Do not bypass unsuccessful calibration or alter service-level calibration values without appropriate authorization and documentation. Expected outcome: Calibration completes normally. If it succeeds, proceed to independent functional verification.

steps.title: 8. Verify Oxygen Delivery Independently
steps.instructions: Using approved calibrated test equipment, compare delivered oxygen concentration under an appropriate test setup. Expected outcome: Delivered oxygen is consistent with the ventilator setting within the acceptance criteria specified by the appropriate manufacturer or facility procedure. Troubleshooting can stop when verification passes.

steps.title: 9. Compare External Components and Gas Sources
steps.instructions: If readings remain questionable, repeat testing with verified gas sources and known-good external hoses or breathing-system components where appropriate. Expected outcome: External gas delivery and removable components are definitively ruled in or out.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Oxygen Measurement Problems
steps.instructions: If calibration continues to fail or independent testing shows unreliable oxygen delivery after external causes are eliminated, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator remains unavailable for clinical use pending qualified evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 displayed an oxygen concentration inconsistent with the selected setting.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the oxygen supply hose was not fully connected at the wall source.
CCR.Resolution: The oxygen connection was secured, oxygen calibration completed successfully, and delivered FiO2 was verified with approved test equipment before return to service.

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - System Check or Pre-Use Check Failure
description: Addresses failed or incomplete pre-use checks caused by circuit setup, accessories, gas supply, external connections, configuration, or equipment faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Ventilation
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a ventilator that cannot complete required checks while a patient depends on it. If the device is in clinical use and reliability is uncertain, transfer ventilation to another verified ventilator or appropriate backup method. Remove the Evita V600 from clinical use until the cause is identified and required verification is completed. Expected outcome: Patient ventilation remains uninterrupted and troubleshooting is performed on an isolated device.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Failed Check
steps.instructions: Repeat the reported condition only when safe and note which portion of the system or pre-use check does not complete. Record any displayed message exactly as shown. Determine whether the failure occurs consistently or only with a particular circuit, accessory, or configuration. Expected outcome: The specific failed stage or condition is identified. If the check now completes normally and the device passes required verification, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Breathing Circuit Setup
steps.instructions: Verify that the breathing circuit is completely assembled, connected to the correct inspiratory and expiratory paths, and free of obvious disconnections, kinks, cracks, loose fittings, or incorrect components. Check water traps, humidification components, filters, and other externally installed accessories for incorrect positioning or obstruction. Expected outcome: The breathing system is complete, correctly assembled, and unobstructed. If correcting the circuit allows the system check to pass, troubleshooting can stop after final verification.

steps.title: 4. Verify the Expiratory Valve and Flow-Sensing Components
steps.instructions: Inspect externally accessible expiratory valve and flow-sensing components for correct installation, secure seating, contamination, moisture, physical damage, or incomplete connection. Do not disassemble components beyond normal approved removal and installation procedures. Expected outcome: All externally removable respiratory components are correctly installed and recognized. If reseating or replacing an approved component restores the check, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 5. Verify Air and Oxygen Supply
steps.instructions: Confirm that required gas supplies are connected and available. Inspect hoses and fittings for loose connections, damage, pinching, or incorrect attachment. If facility gas supply is questionable, compare operation using another verified source when permitted by facility procedure. Expected outcome: Required gas sources are available and stable. If restoring an external gas connection clears the failure, troubleshooting can stop after verification.

steps.title: 6. Check Electrical Power and Basic Startup
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is connected to a known-good AC source and that the power cord and accessible connectors are secure and undamaged. Observe startup for abnormal resets, incomplete booting, unexpected power transitions, or other indications that could interfere with the check. Expected outcome: The ventilator powers normally and remains stable throughout the check.

steps.title: 7. Verify Required Accessories and Configuration
steps.instructions: Confirm that installed breathing-system accessories match the intended clinical configuration and that no recently changed component has introduced an incompatibility or setup problem. Compare with another correctly configured Evita V600 when available rather than making unsupported configuration changes. Expected outcome: The physical setup and selected configuration agree. If correcting an external configuration mismatch restores the check, troubleshooting can stop after verification.

steps.title: 8. Substitute Known-Good External Components
steps.instructions: When appropriate, substitute known-good approved components one at a time, such as the breathing circuit, flow-sensing component, expiratory valve assembly, gas hose, or other removable accessory associated with the failed check. Changing one item at a time helps identify the cause without masking multiple problems. Expected outcome: The system check completes with the known-good component. Replace the defective external component and continue to final verification.

steps.title: 9. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: Repeat the complete required system or pre-use check after corrections. Verify normal ventilation using appropriate test equipment or a test lung and confirm that alarms and monitored values respond appropriately. Expected outcome: The ventilator completes required checks and demonstrates stable, expected operation. Troubleshooting can stop and the device may be returned to service according to facility policy.

steps.title: 10. Escalate an Unresolved Failure
steps.instructions: If the check continues to fail after external setup, gas supply, connections, and removable components have been verified, stop troubleshooting at the external level. Expected outcome: The unresolved ventilator is prevented from returning to clinical use pending qualified service evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 would not complete the pre-use system check.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the expiratory breathing-system component was not fully seated, preventing successful completion of the check.
CCR.Resolution: The component was correctly reseated, the system check was repeated successfully, and ventilator operation was verified with a test lung before return to service.

helpfulDetails: Exact failed check or displayed message

title: Drager Evita V600 Ventilator - Touchscreen, Display, or Rotary Control Unresponsive
description: Addresses unresponsive controls or display problems caused by temporary software conditions, contamination, accessories, power instability, or internal interface faults.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Control of Ventilation
steps.instructions: An unresponsive control interface can prevent safe adjustment or monitoring of ventilation. If the ventilator cannot be reliably controlled, move the patient to another verified ventilator before troubleshooting. Do not continue using a ventilator merely because current settings remain active if controls are unreliable. Expected outcome: The patient is no longer dependent on equipment with an unreliable user interface.

steps.title: 2. Confirm Which Interface Is Affected
steps.instructions: Determine whether the touchscreen, visual display, rotary control, or multiple controls are affected. Identify whether the screen is blank, frozen, delayed, intermittently responsive, or displaying normally while inputs fail. Expected outcome: The specific interface failure is documented.

steps.title: 3. Inspect for External Contamination or Obstruction
steps.instructions: Inspect the touchscreen and control surfaces for fluids, residue, adhesive material, protective coverings, or objects that may interfere with normal operation. Check that no accessory or mounting hardware is pressing against the screen or controls. Expected outcome: Control surfaces are clean and unobstructed. If removing the interference restores reliable control, continue to functional verification.

steps.title: 4. Verify Stable AC Power
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a known-good AC source and inspect the power cord and accessible connections. Note any resets, dimming, flickering, or behavior that coincides with power changes. Expected outcome: The ventilator receives stable external power without abnormal display behavior.

steps.title: 5. Check for a Temporary Software Freeze
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use, perform a normal shutdown and restart if the interface allows it and facility procedures permit. Do not repeatedly power-cycle a device that fails to boot correctly. Expected outcome: The interface restarts and remains responsive. If normal operation is restored, continue testing before return to service.

steps.title: 6. Verify All Available Normal Controls
steps.instructions: Test the touchscreen, rotary control, and other normal operator controls individually. Look for a pattern indicating one localized control problem versus a broader system freeze. Expected outcome: All controls respond consistently and appropriately.

steps.title: 7. Inspect External Connections and Accessories
steps.instructions: Inspect externally connected accessories or communication connections that were added shortly before the problem began. Disconnect only nonessential accessories when the device is off patient and when permitted, then retest. Expected outcome: The interface operates normally without a problematic external accessory, if one was contributing to the condition.

steps.title: 8. Observe for Intermittent Failure
steps.instructions: Operate the ventilator off patient using a test lung and normal controls for a sufficient functional evaluation period. Do not return the device to service if the interface freezes, flickers, or becomes unresponsive even intermittently. Expected outcome: Controls remain stable throughout testing.

steps.title: 9. Complete Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: Verify that ventilation can be configured and adjusted normally, displayed information remains visible, controls respond reliably, and alarms can be acknowledged or managed through normal functions. Expected outcome: The user interface operates consistently and ventilation remains stable. Troubleshooting can stop when required checks pass.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent or Intermittent Interface Failure
steps.instructions: If the touchscreen, display, or rotary control remains unreliable after basic external checks and normal restart, stop troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator is removed from service for qualified repair evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported that the Evita V600 touchscreen stopped responding while the display remained visible.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found dried residue on the touchscreen surface that interfered with consistent touch response.
CCR.Resolution: The screen was cleaned using the approved external cleaning process, all controls were functionally tested, and ventilation was verified with a test lung before return to service.

helpfulDetails: Touchscreen, display, rotary control, or multiple controls affected
Blank, frozen, flickering, or intermittent behavior

title: Drager Evita V800 Ventilator - Air or O2 Gas Supply Failure
description: Addresses loss or instability of medical air or oxygen caused by wall supply, hoses, connections, fittings, or related external gas-source conditions.

steps.title: 1. Maintain Safe Patient Ventilation
steps.instructions: Treat any loss of ventilator gas supply as a potentially urgent patient-support issue. If a patient is connected, provide immediate ventilation and oxygen using another verified ventilator or appropriate backup method. Do not troubleshoot unreliable gas delivery while the patient depends on the affected unit. Expected outcome: The patient is continuously ventilated with a dependable gas source.

steps.title: 2. Identify Which Supply Is Affected
steps.instructions: Determine whether the ventilator reports loss of: Medical air Oxygen Both supplies An intermittent or low-supply condition Record any displayed message and the conditions immediately preceding the failure. Expected outcome: The affected gas path is identified. If the alarm clears after a confirmed temporary infrastructure interruption and all functions verify normally, troubleshooting can stop after documentation.

steps.title: 3. Inspect Wall Connections
steps.instructions: Verify each gas hose is fully inserted into the correct wall outlet or source connection. Confirm oxygen and air have not been crossed. Inspect the outlet engagement for obvious looseness or incomplete connection. Expected outcome: Both gas hoses are connected to their correct sources. If securing the connection restores normal gas status, perform functional verification and troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 4. Inspect Ventilator Hose Connections
steps.instructions: Confirm the air and oxygen hoses are securely connected at the ventilator. Look for loose fittings, damaged connectors, contamination, or evidence of impact. Do not use damaged gas fittings. Expected outcome: Both hoses are securely connected and physically intact. If correction restores the supply, troubleshooting can stop after completing the applicable check.

steps.title: 5. Inspect Hoses Along Their Full Accessible Length
steps.instructions: Check each hose for: Kinking Crushing Sharp bends Cuts Abrasion Damaged fittings Obvious leakage Equipment or furniture restricting the hose Expected outcome: The gas hoses have an unobstructed path and no visible damage. If repositioning or replacing a damaged hose restores normal operation, complete verification and troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 6. Verify Facility Gas Source
steps.instructions: Test or compare the suspected wall outlet using an appropriate facility-approved method or another known-good outlet. If multiple devices on the same source show similar problems, consider an infrastructure issue rather than a ventilator fault. Expected outcome: The facility gas source is confirmed available. If the outlet is the problem, move the ventilator to a verified source and refer the infrastructure condition to the appropriate department.

steps.title: 7. Test With Known-Good Compatible Gas Hoses
steps.instructions: When necessary, substitute a known-good compatible air or oxygen hose one at a time. Expected outcome: Normal gas recognition returns with a known-good hose or the external hose is ruled out. If a hose is defective, remove it from service and complete ventilator verification.

steps.title: 8. Verify Gas Recognition During System Check
steps.instructions: With the ventilator off the patient and both verified sources connected, perform the applicable system or pre-use check. Expected outcome: Both air and oxygen supplies are recognized without unresolved alarms. If the check passes, proceed to final functional verification.

steps.title: 9. Perform Functional Verification
steps.instructions: Operate the ventilator on approved test equipment or a suitable test lung according to facility practice. Confirm ventilation remains stable and gas-related alarms do not recur. Expected outcome: The ventilator maintains normal operation using verified air and oxygen supplies. Troubleshooting can stop and the unit may be returned to service.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Persistent Gas-Supply Recognition Failure
steps.instructions: If a verified gas source and known-good hose remain unrecognized, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The device remains removed from clinical use pending qualified bench evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported the Evita V800 displayed an oxygen supply failure when connected in the patient room.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the oxygen hose fitting was incompletely engaged at the wall outlet.
CCR.Resolution: Clinical Engineering reconnected the oxygen hose securely, confirmed both gas supplies were recognized, completed the system check and functional test, and returned the ventilator to service.

title: Drager Evita V800 Ventilator - Apnea, Low Minute Volume, or Low Tidal Volume Alarm
description: Addresses low-volume or apnea alarms related to patient conditions, disconnections, leaks, circuit problems, settings, sensing, or ventilation performance.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Confirm Ventilation
steps.instructions: Apnea, low minute volume, and low tidal volume alarms can indicate inadequate patient ventilation. Clinical staff must immediately assess the patient, airway, and actual ventilation. If reliable ventilation is in doubt, use another verified ventilator or appropriate backup ventilation method before technical troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The patient receives dependable ventilation independently of the suspect device.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Alarm Condition
steps.instructions: Ask clinical staff which alarm occurred and whether it was: Apnea Low minute volume Low tidal volume A combination of these alarms Intermittent or continuous Record the displayed message, therapy mode, and circumstances when reported. Expected outcome: The exact reported condition is defined. If the event is clearly patient-related and the ventilator passes controlled testing, troubleshooting can stop after documentation.

steps.title: 3. Inspect for Circuit Disconnection
steps.instructions: Check all breathing circuit connections from the ventilator to the test interface. Look for loose fittings, disconnected limbs, open ports, poorly seated accessories, or components that separate under movement. Expected outcome: The circuit is complete and secure. If correcting a disconnection resolves the alarm during testing, troubleshooting can stop after final verification.

steps.title: 4. Inspect for Significant Leaks
steps.instructions: Check the circuit, humidification components, test lung connection, and accessories for visible damage or leaks. Verify caps and ports are properly closed where appropriate. Use compatible known-good circuit components when necessary. Expected outcome: No significant external leak is present. If a damaged external component caused the low-volume condition, replace it and complete functional verification.

steps.title: 5. Inspect Flow-Sensing and Expiratory Components
steps.instructions: Verify applicable flow-sensing components and the expiratory valve are correctly seated, recognized, clean, dry, and free of visible damage. Expected outcome: External flow-measurement components are properly installed. If reseating or replacing a component restores accurate volume detection, complete the applicable system check and troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 6. Review Ventilation and Alarm Settings
steps.instructions: With authorized clinical personnel as appropriate, review the mode, delivered support settings, apnea-related configuration, and alarm limits reported during the event. Do not alter patient therapy settings solely to silence an alarm. Expected outcome: The alarm configuration and ventilation settings are understood and appropriate for controlled evaluation. If an unintended setting is identified and corrected by authorized personnel, verify normal device operation.

steps.title: 7. Test With a Known-Good Circuit and Test Lung
steps.instructions: Connect a compatible known-good circuit and suitable test lung or approved ventilator tester. Operate the ventilator under controlled conditions. Expected outcome: The ventilator delivers and measures breaths consistently without inappropriate apnea or low-volume alarms. If successful, the original circuit or patient interface is the more likely external source.

steps.title: 8. Verify Flow and Volume Performance
steps.instructions: When required, use approved ventilator test equipment to compare delivered and measured ventilation parameters against applicable manufacturer or facility acceptance criteria. Expected outcome: Ventilation and volume measurement meet approved criteria. If they do, continue to final alarm verification.

steps.title: 9. Verify Alarm Operation
steps.instructions: Using an approved test method, confirm applicable apnea and low-volume alarms activate when the simulated condition is created and clear when normal ventilation is restored. Expected outcome: The alarms respond appropriately and the ventilator demonstrates normal function. Troubleshooting can stop and the unit may be returned to service.

steps.title: 10. Escalate Unresolved Low-Volume or Apnea Conditions
steps.instructions: If the alarm recurs with a known-good circuit and test lung, or delivered and measured ventilation cannot be verified, stop external troubleshooting. Expected outcome: The ventilator remains removed from service for qualified bench evaluation.
